newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COCOA - Farmers show little interest in new strain.
newsitem.headline: COCOA - Farmers show little interest in new strain.

text.p: The Brazilian government has begun distribution of a new strain of cocoa plant which it says has been shown to be more productive and have higher resistance to witch's broom disease than existing strains.
However, researchers at the government's cocoa institute (Ceplac) say that initial response from farmers has been slow.
Distribution of the new strain, called Theobahia, began late last year, said Raul Valle, head of research at the Ceplac offices in Itabuna, in the heart of the cocoa growing region of Bahia.
Valle said that tests had shown that the incidence of witch's broom in pods of Theobahia plants was approximately one to two percent of that in plants currently cultivated in the growing region.
Productivity was around 120 15-kilo arrobas per hectare compared to 15 to 20 arrobas at present, he added.
Valle said Theobahia was the result of nearly two decades of experiments and that tests had been conducted over the last three years, firstly in greenhouses and then in the field.
He said Theobahia trees would start producing some fruits three years after being planted, reaching their full potential another three years later.

Ceplac had initially made Theobahia seeds available at its headquarters but very few farmers showed any interest. The insitute then decided to take the seeds to farmers and millions have since been distributed.

Farmers said the somewhat lukewarm response was due to low morale following what they said had been years of falling world prices, unfavourable weather, the spread of witch's broom disease and lack of co-operation from the government.
"Farmers are totally demoralised," said cocoa farmer Ronaldo Monteiro.
"They do not want to plant cocoa any more. They are diversifying, turning to other crops and to cattle."
He said that some were waiting to see how another strain, currently the subject of experiments by food manufacturers Nestle, would develop.

The strain, CNN51, has been brought from Ecuador, where it has been found to be more resistant to witch's broom, and is being tested in Itabuna to see if it can thrive in the different climate and soil of Bahia.
"Cocoa trees are a long term investment and so farmers are very cautious about what they plant," Monteiro said.
Internal prices for cocoa were around 20 Real per arroba this week.
Producers said that weather had been good for cocoa, with abundant rainfall, but that this was too late to help the current October-April main crop, which has been ravaged by drought.
The main crop is expected to produce around 1.0 million 60 kilo bags.
